extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, media researchers, and students studying news selection and newsworthiness
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual dimensions useful for evaluating or producing news items (and predicting their placement/engagement) based on Schramm's 1949 account of news as a reconstructed product and his immediate-vs-delayed reader-reward distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward Type (immediate vs delayed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes stories by the kind of reward they give readers: Immediate-reward news generates quick gratification (crime, accidents, disasters, sports, social events, human interest) where the reader gets emotional payoff at the time of reading; Delayed-reward news (public affairs, economic news, science, education, public health) requires cognitive effort from the reader for eventual benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schramm argues newsrooms over-produce immediate-reward news because it is easier to package and reliably engages readers; delayed-reward stories require more effort from producer and consumer. For measurement: immediate-vs-delayed reward can be coded for any story and used as a content-feature predictor of homepage placement and engagement. Examples: crime story = immediate; policy analysis = delayed. Anti-pattern: treating all civic/public affairs stories as equally 'newsworthy' without accounting for their delayed payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical Fit / Mechanical demands of transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that fit established technical/format constraints — column inches, broadcast slots, page layout, word counts — are favored in selection and packaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical demands of transmission shape length, form, emphasis and interpretation; stories that slot easily into these constraints 'win' selection battles. Practical implication: craft stories to match typical format lengths and broadcast slots for higher placement probability. Anti-pattern: producing stories that require atypical length or format that editors must substantially rework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predisposition Compatibility (reporter bias and knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter's own knowledge, beliefs and predispositions filter source selection and shape how events are reconstructed into news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schramm lists the reporter's own knowledge and predispositions among the building blocks of news; this implies that source selection, emphasis, and framing will reflect personal biases. For evaluation: examine source choices and framing for alignment with reporter predispositions. Anti-pattern: assuming neutrality of reconstruction; failure to disclose or correct for reporter bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Anticipation (editors' model of readers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors' anticipations or models of audience needs and preferences shape which stories are selected and how they are presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is shaped by anticipated needs/preferences of audience — what readers want influences emphasis and choice. For homepage placement, prioritize stories aligned with the outlet's perceived audience reward profile. Anti-pattern: assigning prominence to stories that editorial leadership believes audiences don't value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Customer Demand (buyers of news: wire customers, advertisers, subscribers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wishes and demands of buyers of news (wire-service customers, editors, advertisers) influence which stories are produced and highlighted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlets and wire services cater to subscriber preferences; customer demand can drive selection and prominence. Modern analogue: recommender-system feedback loops and commercial incentives. For producers: consider buyer/subscriber priorities when pitching or placing stories. Anti-pattern: ignoring commercial/customer constraints when predicting placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as Reconstruction (news ≠ raw event)
rubrics_metrics.description: News is a reconstruction of events, built from eyewitness accounts, secondhand accounts, tertiary commentary, and the reporter's own knowledge and predispositions, then coded and modified by people unconnected to the original event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that reporting is an interpretive process — length, form, emphasis, and interpretation are altered to meet mechanical, audience, and customer constraints. For production: corroborate across sources and be explicit about provenance; for evaluation: assess how reconstruction choices (which sources used, how coded) may have altered the original event's meaning. Anti-pattern: treating news copy as a verbatim account of events without considering intervening transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit with Packaging/Production Ease (ease of packaging drives selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that are easier to package and transmit (in terms of format, narrative simplicity, and immediate emotional payoff) are more likely to be produced and prioritized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schramm notes that immediate-reward stories are easier to package and thus over-produced. When evaluating or producing content for high placement, prefer narratives that are concise, emotionally immediate, and compatible with production workflows. Anti-pattern: favoring complex, effortful-to-explain stories when predicting or seeking front-page/homepage prominence.
